case_name: Children’s Aid Society of Toronto v. T.G.
text:
WARNING

The court hearing this matter directs
that the following notice should be attached to the file:

This
is a case under Part III of the
Child and Family Services Act
and is
subject to one or more of subsections 48(7), 45(8) and 45(9) of the Act.
These subsections and subsection 85(3)
of the
Child and Family Services Act
,
which deals with the consequences of failure to
comply, read as follows:

45.—
(7)
Order
excluding media representatives or prohibiting publication.
—   The
court may make an order,

.   .   .

(
c
)    prohibiting the
publication of a report of the hearing or a specified part of the hearing,

where the court is of the opinion that
. . .  publication of the report,  . . .,
would cause emotional harm to a child who is a witness at or a participant in
the hearing or is the subject of the proceeding.

(8)
Prohibition:
identifying child.
—   No person shall publish or make public
information that has the effect of identifying a child who is a witness at or a
participant in a hearing or the subject of a proceeding, or the child's parent
or foster parent or a member of the child's family.

(9)
Idem: order re
adult.
—   The court may make an order prohibiting the publication
of information that has the effect of identifying a person charged with an offence
under this Part.

.

.   .

85.—
(3)
Idem.
—   A person who
contravenes subsection 45(8) or 76(11) (publication of identifying information)
or an order prohibiting publication made under clause 45(7)(
c
) or
subsection 45(9), and a director, officer or employee of a corporation who
authorizes, permits or concurs in such a contravention by the corporation, is
guilty of an offence and on conviction is liable to a fine of not more than
$10,000 or to imprisonment for a term of not more than three years, or to both.

COURT FILE No.:  Toronto C50456/10

DATE:  2011·03-02

Citation:
Children’s Aid Society of
Toronto v. T.G.
,  2011 ONCJ 625

ONTARIO
COURT  OF  JUSTICE

BETWEEN:

Children’s Aid Society of Toronto,

Applicant,

—  AND  —

Ms. T.G. and Mr. D.S.,

Respondents.

Before Justice Marvin A. Zuker

Trial heard on February
7, 8, 9, and 10, 2011

Reasons for
Judgment released on 2 March 2011

Anthony Macri  ...........................................................................................   for
the applicant society

Glen Cook  ..............................................................................................   for
the respondent mother

Nafisa Nazarali  .........................................................................................   for
the respondent father

ZUKER, J.:

[
1
]

Pursuant to a child protection application
filed March 1, 2010, the Society seeks a finding that pursuant to section 37 of
the
Child and Family Services Act
that:

[
2
]

There is a risk that the children, Ha.S. and
Si.S., are likely to suffer physical harm, inflicted by the person having
charge of the children or caused by that person’s:

•

failure to care for, provide for, supervise or
protect the children adequately [subclause 37(2)(b)(i)] and

•

pattern of neglect in caring for, providing for,
supervising or protecting the children [subclause 37(2)(b)(ii)].

[
3
]

The children’s parent has died or is
unavailable to exercise his or her custodial rights over the children and has
not made adequate provision for the children’s care and custody [clause
37(2)(i)].

[
4
]

The family consists of:

1. Ms.
T.G., the biological mother, born July […], 1988;

2. Mr. D.S.,
the biological father, born December […], 1981;

3. Ha.S.,
3-year-old child, born October […], 2007;

4. Si.S.,
2-year-old child, born November […], 2008; and

5. Mrs.
C., maternal grandmother and proposed caregiver.

[
5
]

The Society was involved with the G./S.
family in 2009, due to concerns relating to domestic violence by Mr. D.S.
against Ms. T.G., Ms. T.G.’s minimization and/or denial at times of domestic
violence, its impact on the children, the parents’ drinking, criminal charges
faced by both parents, and their lack of parenting skills.

[
6
]

Jastinder Manchanda, the Family Services
Worker, states in part, in her affidavit dated February 2, 2011 and filed as
Exhibit 3 during these proceedings:

Previous involvement with the
Society

[
7
]

“The Society attempted to work on a
voluntary basis with the family for a period of approximately 12 months
(February to March 2009, March to May 2009, and again in July 2009 to February
2010), to address various concerns and ensure the ongoing safety and well-being
of the two young children in the home.

[
8
]

“In March 2009, Toronto police reported
another domestic incident to the Society.  Ms. T.G. advised the Society that there
had been an altercation between her and Mr. D.S. after a round of heavy
drinking, and that Mr. D.S. fled the scene in an unlicensed vehicle but was
later stopped by the police.  He was placed in police custody and charged with
six (6) offences including Assault and Driving Under the Influence.  Due to his
prior criminal record and a number of occurrences of Failure to Comply, Mr.
D.S. was denied bail and remained incarcerated for a period of time.

[
9
]

“In July 2009, the Society became involved
with the family again, following a report by Ms. T.G. that Mr. D.S. was
excessively drinking and being verbally abusive to her (when he got drunk, he
called her names and became “mean”), that their arguments were increasing in
frequency and impacting the children, and that their daughter witnessed the
incident and cried.  She wanted to know her rights.”

Current involvement

[
10
]

“I assumed carriage of this file on
September 29, 2009.  At that time, I attended a transfer meeting with Raquel
Britton, Intake Worker and the family, at their family home.

[
11
]

“On October 22, 2009, I received a new
referral from Police Constable Verma through the Society’s Screening Department
about a domestic incident in the G./S. family that occurred on October 19, 2009
and continued on October 22, 2009.  PC Verma advised the Society of the
following:

a.

Ms. T.G. and Mr. D.S. were name-calling and Mr.
D.S. punched Ms. T.G. on her jaw;

b.

Mr. D.S. told Ms. T.G. that he won’t assault her
but will get some [one] to take care of her;

c.

Mr. D.S. threw the apartment keys and left the
apartment;

d.

The keys contained a key to a storage room and
when Ms. T.G. opened the storage room, she found 7 marijuana plants inside;

e.

Ms. T.G. called the police to report the assault
and that she found 7 marijuana plants inside the storage room of her apartment;

f.

The male could not be located and the Police
laid a warrant to arrest Mr. D.S. for domestic assault, threaten death and
possession for the purpose of.

[
12
]

“I then called police for assistance in my
investigation and two police officers from Division 23 joined me to assist me
in my investigation.  Mr. Laird had to leave as he was ill.  When the police
arrived Ms. T.G. allowed me entry to the apartment to see and meet with the
children.  Then I observed the following:

a.

Ms. T.G. was nervous but cooperative at that
time.

b.

The marijuana plants had been already cleaned up
by the police officers.

c.

The grow-op paraphernalia was still there in the
storage room which included electrical wires, bulbs, exhaust fan, water pipes
for creating temporary irrigation system, big sheets of tin foil to magnifying
light.

d.

The storage room had been filled with children’s
extra toys and little bikes.

e.

When asked how she could not know that there was
a grow-op in her home, Ms. T.G. said that she did not hear the noise of the fan
and that Mr. D.S. kept that room locked all the time and she was not able to
get in there.

f.

Ms. T.G. advised that Mr. D.S. had been on the
run since.

[
13
]

“During the period that I was involved with
the family, I assessed and identified numerous child protection concerns
including:

a.

Domestic violence by Mr. D.S. against Ms. T.G.;

b.

Ms. T.G.’s minimization of the domestic violence
problem;

c.

The parents’ excessive drinking; and

d.

Poor parenting skills, immaturity and
impulsivity and repeated involvement in the criminal justice system.

[
14
]

“While I attempted to work with the family,
I experienced a poor level of cooperation by Ms. T.G.  I had difficulty in
arranging home visits and Ms. T.G. would not follow through with service
referrals.  In November 2009, Mr. D.S. was incarcerated and remained in jail
until the end of March 2010.

[
15
]

“Additional concerns were identified, as a
marijuana grow-operation was discovered in the family home in October 2009, and
a warrant was issued for Mr. D.S.’s arrest.

[
16
]

“His whereabouts were unknown for a period
of time, but he was eventually located, arrested on another charge of assault,
and incarcerated at Maplehurst Detention Centre in and around November 2009.

[
17
]

“Ms. T.G. subsequently revealed that she had
been incarcerated for a period of time in December 2009 on criminal charges
relating to fraud and forgery.

[
18
]

“Between December 2009 and January 2010, Ms.
T.G.’s level of cooperation with the Society began to deteriorate and she
cancelled a number of scheduled visits.

[
19
]

“On February 23, 2010, the Society
apprehended the children, Ha.S. and Si.S., following a police report that Ms.
T.G. had been arrested and incarcerated, after a firearm was discovered in the
home.  The apartment was also found to be in a highly unsafe and unsanitary
state.

[
20
]

“Ms. T.G. was charged following this
incident.  At the time, Mr. D.S. was already in detention.

[
21
]

“Ms. T.G. was incarcerated from February 23
to March 5, 2010.

[
22
]

“As of March 1, 2010, both parents remained
incarcerated.  Ms. T.G. was denied bail at her criminal hearing on February 26,
2010.

[
23
]

“On the evening of February 23, 2010, Ms.
T.G. was charged with the following:

a.

Careless Storage of firearms;

b.

Unauthorized possession of a firearm;

c.

Possession of a firearm, knowing its possession
is unauthorized; and

d.

Possession of firearms obtained by the
commission of an offence.

[
24
]

“Ms. T.G.’s charges from Peel Region dated
April 16, 2010 were as follows:

a.

Forged Documents;

b.

Fraud Under, contrary to
s. 380(1)
of the
Criminal
Code
; and

c.

Fraudulent Use of Credit Cards.

[
25
]

“Ms. T.G. was sentenced to a conditional
sentence of 4 months arising from these charges from Peel Police.

[
26
]

“Ms. T.G. at this time was living with Mrs.
C. who is her primary Surety.

[
27
]

“Ms. T.G. was re-arrested on two occasions
for breach of bail conditions during the period from March 24 to April 22,
2010.  Ms. T.G. also has outstanding charges from Brampton jurisdiction
relating to fraud occurring from December 2009.

[
28
]

“The Society could not approve Mrs. C.’s,
for a number of reasons, including the fact that Ms. T.G. would be residing
with her and that she would be the effective caregiver to the children.  If Mrs.
C. would rescind her surety and require that Ms. T.G. move out, the Society
could then continue to assess Mrs. C.’s plan.  On a number of occasions both
Ms. T.G. and Mrs. C. were advised of the Society’s requirement.

[
29
]

“Pursuant to a Notice of Motion on March 1,
2010, the Society sought an order placing the children, Si.S., born November
27, 2008, and Ha.S., born October 1, 2007, in the temporary care and custody of
the Children’s Aid Society of Toronto, with access at the discretion of the
Children’s Aid Society of Toronto, pending the disposition of the Protection
Application.”

[
30
]

Pursuant to the affidavit of Paul Burke, the
Family Service Worker, dated February 2, 2011, filed as Exhibit 6 to these
proceedings:

Intake/Apprehension

[
31
]

“On or about February 23, 2010, I became
aware of the G./S. family in carrying out my duties as an “Emergency Coverage
Worker” for my team because the assigned Family Service Worker for this family,
Jastinder Manchanda, was not available to respond to the crisis.  In my duties
as Emergency Coverage Worker on this day, I had to follow up on a report from
the 22 Division police that they were with Ha.S. and Si.S. at their family’s
apartment and that their mother had been arrested and there was nobody to care
for the girls.

[
32
]

“As a result of this information at 11:15
a.m. I went to the family home at 2737 Kipling Ave. accompanied by Society Case
Aide Maria Boholy following a report of Ms. T.G.’s arrest and subsequent
incarceration.  Upon arrival Ms. Boholy and I were greeted in the hallway
outside apartment #211 by Police Constables Ho and Thomas who advised us of the
following:

a.

Ms. T.G. was incarcerated.

b.

The 2 children, Ha.S. and Si.S. were both sleeping
together in a playpen and that the environmental condition of the apartment was
terrible, more specifically that there was cat feces on the floor, numerous
soiled diapers strewn around the apartment mixed with clothes and food crumbs
on almost all areas of the floor and furniture and there was vomit on the
couch.

c.

PC Thomas confirmed that there also was a
22-calibre handgun on top of the refrigerator and that there were a lot of
crack cocaine pipes and other equipment strewn around the bathroom.

d.

There also was a dildo and a used condom on the
floor of the bathroom.

e.

He further explained that they were awaiting a
warrant to search the apartment and as such nothing was to be taken from the
home.

f.

PC Thomas obtained the children’s Health Cards
prior to the mother’s being taken into custody and he gave them both to me.

g.

PC Thomas advised that one of the 2 bedroom
doors was closed to keep the family cat contained.  I overheard it meowing
constantly behind the door.

[
33
]

“Both children also were very hungry and
food was prepared for them both.  The eldest child Ha.S. was concerned for her
sister and wanted to ensure that Si.S. was given food by pushing a staff
member’s hands with a baby bottle toward her younger sister and directing them
to put it in her mouth.  Ha.S. in the meantime demonstrated a hearty appetite
and she ate and drank lots of the food provided.  In terms of the children’s
physical development it was observed that Ha.S. (28 months old) was able to
walk independently but that Si.S. (15 months old) was still unable to walk
independently and was “roaming” the furniture.

[
34
]

“In combination of the unsafe/unsanitary
conditions of the family home at the time of the girls’ apprehension, substance
use by the parents and drug paraphernalia in the home, a sample of the children’s
hair was taken from each of the girls at the time of this Admission Medical and
was submitted to Motherisk Program at the Hospital for Sick Children for
screening.  The results of these hair samples indicated that both girls were
found to be positive for cocaine over a continued period of eight-and-one-half
months.  Attached as Exhibit “C” to this affidavit is a true copy of the
children’s hair strand tests.

[
35
]

“On February 18, 2010, Tanya Walker from the
Peel Children’s Aid Society sent a new referral report to the Society advising
to apprise me, being the current worker to Ms. T.G.  The report read the
following:

a.

It had received a referral from a counsellor in
Alberta the night before that Ms. T.G. had contacted the counsellor and
disclosed being abused by her stepfather.

b.

Ms. T.G. was concerned that her 15-year-old
sister might be being abused at present and that her sister resided in Peel.

c.

The stepfather’s name is Narinder C.

d.

The police and the Peel CAS conducted
interviews; however, Ms. T.G. retracted her statement.

[
36
]

“On February 18, 2010, the Society received
a call from Tanya Walker, who identified herself as an employee from Peel CAS
and reported as follows:

[
37
]

“Ms. T.G. had contacted a counsellor in
Alberta, disclosed that she had been abused by her stepfather, and expressed
her worry that her 15-year-old sister who lived in the home might also be being
abused.

[
38
]

“The Peel CAS and police had initiated
interviews, but Ms. T.G. subsequently retracted her statement.”

[
39
]

“During the course of these proceedings,
access has been scheduled on Wednesdays and Fridays for 1.5 hours separately to
the father and the mother, respectively.  Mrs. C. had regular access along with
Ms. T.G., since Ms. T.G. was required to be accompanied by her surety at all
times.

[
40
]

“To assist the parents with structured
access visits, it was suggested to the parents that they use the first thirty
minutes of the visits for stimulating play or developmental activity; the next
30 minutes for eating; and the last 30 minutes for cognitive activity time
including reading or puzzles, etc.  These expectations were expressed to the
parents on a number of occasions.  Contrary to the clear expectations and
redirection, forced feeding throughout the visit was the dominant activity.
The parents frequently failed to follow the cues of the children and when the
children said “full,” the feeding still continued.”

[
41
]

The Society filed a Plan of Care on April
28, 2010.

[
42
]

“The details of the order we ask the court
to make are as follows:

That the
children, Ha.S. and Si.S., be made Wards of the Children’s Aid Society of
Toronto for a period of six months.

That
access between the children and their parents be at the Society’s discretion,
and in accordance with any criminal court conditions imposed on the parents.

[
43
]

“The children’s aid society expects the
respondents to carry out certain conditions before it would feel that
supervision or wardship for the children is no longer needed.  Very serious
consequences could result if those conditions are broken.  These conditions
are:

a.

Ms. T.G. and Mr. D.S. shall demonstrate that
they are no longer abusing drugs and alcohol, or involved in drug trafficking
or drug grow-operations in their own residence(s) or elsewhere.

b.

Ms. T.G. and Mr. D.S. shall not at any time
possess, use or have access to a firearm, whether in their residence(s),
vehicle(s) or in the community.

c.

Ms. T.G. and Mr. D.S. shall participate and
cooperate in a psychological or psychiatric assessment, as referred to by the
Society, and followed through with all recommendations arising from the
assessment.

d.

Ms. T.G. and Mr. D.S. shall undergo drug and
alcohol testing, as may be requested by the Society.

e.

Ms. T.G. and Mr. D.S. shall attend at and
complete parenting program(s), as referred to by the Society, and demonstrate
appropriate progress and an ability to implement on a sustained basis the
skills taught to them in such program(s).

f.

Ms. T.G. and Mr. D.S. shall attend at and
complete individual and/or couple’s counselling, as referred to by the Society.

g.

Ms. T.G. and Mr. D.S. shall attend to their
outstanding criminal charges, demonstrate an ability to comply with their bail
or probation conditions without further breach, and keep the Society apprised
of the status of their criminal proceedings and their bail/probation conditions.

h.

Ms. T.G. and Mr. D.S. shall cooperate with the
Society and sign consents as may be requested by the Society to allow the
Society to communicate and exchange information with collaterals involved with
the family.

[
44
]

“The children cannot be adequately protected
while in the care of the respondents.

[
45
]

“Ms. T.G. was released from jail on March 5,
2010 with bail conditions.  Mr. D.S. was released from jail on March 26, 2010.
Towards the end of April 2010, Ms. T.G. was arrested and incarcerated again for
a period of nine days, due to breach of her bail conditions. She did not advise
the Society of this development or otherwise ensure that existing arrangements
for access visits with her children could be put on hold or changed.

[
46
]

“On March 1, 2010, the Honourable Mr.
Justice Spence made an order placing the children in the temporary care and
custody of the Society, with access at the discretion of the Society, having
regard to any existing bail order.

[
47
]

“On June 25, 2010, a Therapeutic Access
Program admission meeting was facilitated and attended by TAP Coordinator
Shannon Deacon, Ms. Manchanda, Ms. T.G., Mr. D.S. and Mrs. C.  The maternal
aunt, Tajinder C., also came but was not allowed to participate.  The TAP
Coordinator, Shannon Deacon, explained the purpose of the program toward
educating care providers and that specifically this family’s attendance would
be to assess a plan for Mr. D.S. to care for the girls with the assistance of Mrs.
C.  It was agreed that Mr. D.S. and Mrs. C. would begin attending the TAP on Friday,
July 16, 2010, and then, following this, they were scheduled to be at TAP two
days per week on Wednesdays from 10:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m. and on Fridays from
10:00 a.m. to 12:30 p.m.  Following Mr. D.S.’s and Mrs. C.’s visits on Fridays,
Ms. T.G. was scheduled to have her visits with the girls from 12:30 to 2:00
p.m.  It was emphasized that mother’s visits are not a part of the TAP
assessment but simply to facilitate access for her to the girls while limiting
the need for additional disruption to the children’s routine by having to have
them attend a third visit during the week.  See Exhibit 6,
supra
.

[
48
]

“Access at the Therapeutic Access Program
(TAP) was scheduled to begin with the family on July 16, 2010.  The purpose of
this initiative was to strengthen Mr. D.S.’s parenting skills and knowledge in
parenting and to support his plan.  Mr. D.S. failed to attend any sessions at
the TAP.

[
49
]

“On July 23, 2010, Ms. T.G. attended for
access, accompanied by Mrs. C. and maternal aunt as part of the plan.  During
the visit, Ms. Deacon, Coordinator from the TAP, observed that Ms. T.G. was
affectionate and remained available to the children; however, she came
ill-prepared to meet their needs.  She was unable to organize their emotional
care when the girls struggled to fall asleep for a nap.

[
50
]

“On June 3, 2010, I contacted Ms. T.G. to
follow up with her progress in following through with the referrals made so
far.  At this time Ms. T.G. advised me of the following:

a.

She completed the first assessment held on June
2 at Jean Tweed but did not provide me the worker’s name;

b.

The second part of the assessment for addiction
treatment was scheduled for the following Tuesday.”

Hair Drug Analysis

[
51
]

“On March 30, 2010, I received the hair test
results for Ha.S. (segmental for 7.5 months) and Si.S. conducted on February
24, 2010.  Attached as Exhibit “B” to this affidavit is a true copy of these
results.  The children tested positive for cocaine and benzolyecgonine. This
period also included the period when Mr. D.S. was living in the family home and
was parenting the children.

[
52
]

“On March 30, 2010, I consulted with Monique
Moller, Laboratory Counsellor at Motherrisk Program, for an interpretation of
hair test results of the children, Ha.S. and Si.S.  Ms. Moller advised me of
the following:

a.

The cocaine in their system was of medium to
medium high range, i.e., 25
th
to 75
th
percentile.

b.

Such amounts were “quite a bit” of cocaine in
the child’s system.

c.

Such a high quantity of cocaine can be due to
either the child’s exposure to drugs in the home environment or drug residue
present in the home or the mother could be abusing a lot of drugs which could
contaminate the child through mother’s sweat.

d.

It was hard to say if the children were not
ingesting the drugs directly.

e.

Inhalation through secondhand smoke from abusers
in the immediate environment is more likely in the present circumstance as it
may be caused by more than one person abusing drugs in the home.

f.

It was concerning how the children got such high
amounts in their system.

g.

Benzoylecgonine is a metabolite of crack
cocaine.

h.

The children can be assessed for possible
medical issues among children if they were exposed to home environments where
drugs are grown, abused or handled.

[
53
]

“On June 29, 2010, Ms. T.G. submitted her
own hair strand sample.  Attached as Exhibit “C” to this affidavit is a true
copy of the hair test results.  The segmental test reported positive for
cocaine and benzoylecgonine for one-year period.  It was particularly high
during the last 6 months dating back and including June.

[
54
]

“On November 26, 2010, Ms. T.G. went for
another hair test analysis.  Attached as Exhibit “D” to this affidavit is a
true copy of the test results with an interpretation by Mr. Gareri, one of the
directors of the Motherisk program.

[
55
]

“Mr. D.S. has failed to submit any hair
sample for a drug analysis to date.”

[
56
]

The Mother’s
Answer and Plan of Care
,
dated May 21, 2010 (see Exhibit 1, Trial Record, at Tab 2), filed May 27, 2010,
states in part:

1.

“Unless expressly agreed to herein, the
respondent mother denies the allegations of the CAS and places it to the strict
proof thereof.

2.   “The
respondent mother is a good conscientious mother.  She admits to having a
downtime in her parenting of the children in and around the time of
apprehension.

3.  “The
mother was not incarcerated for a period of time around December 2009.  She
admits she was charged but was released on a promise to appear.

4.  “The
mother denies that there were domestic violence issues as she and the father,
Mr. D.S., had a rocky relationship where there were arguments but did not give
rise to violence.  The mother admits calling the police on the father to get
back at him for arguments.  She has acknowledged to the courts that she made
the charges up when the charge would go to trial.

5.    “The
apartment was not in such disarray as the pictures suggest, as the pictures
were taken after the police had torn the place up while searching for drugs and
other elements to lay charges.

6.     “The
mother denies that the children were in heavily soiled diapers at the time of
apprehension.  There was plenty of food for the kids in the fridge and the
cupboards.  The children were well fed and, if they were hungry at the time of
apprehension, it was due to the fact it was 7:00 a.m. in the morning and they
had just gotten up and not had the opportunity to be given breakfast.

7.    “The
younger child had a slight diaper rash.  It was not as bad as the pictures
taken as the child was apprehended and the pictures were taken several hours
later and any diaper rash was worsened while under CAS care.

8.   “The
mother was charged as a result of a gun being found.  The mother had no idea
that there was a gun in the apartment.  The gun was hidden on the top of the
back of the fridge.  The police, when they first found the gun, took it out of
the apartment in a zip-lock bag, took it to the police station when they drove
the mother to the station, then came back later with the gun, and took pictures
with the gun being placed on the front of the fridge in open view.

9.   “The
mother was not denied bail on February 26, 2010, she was just remanded to have
her surety attend for a bail hearing.  The mother was granted bail on March 5,
2010.  She is to reside with her mother and cousin, the sureties, in Brampton.

10.   “The
mother asserts that there were difficulties in the matter and agrees that
around the time of apprehension she was in a depressed state and not properly
taking care of herself and the children.

11.   “However,
prior to the New Year of 2010, she was doing well with the children and had
taken action to make sure that the children were doing well.  For example, she
had shown that she had proper cribs for the children.  There were no unsafe

THE LAW

[
196
]

The factors set out in s. 37(3) are subject
to the paramount duty in s. 1 to protect the best interests of an apprehended
child.  Family and parental relationships are to be recognized only to the
extent that they are “consistent with the best interest, protection and
well-being of the children”: see
Syl Apps Secure Treatment Centre v.
D.(B.)
,
2007 SCC 38 (CanLII)
, [2007] S.C.J. No. 38 (S.C.C.).  A plan proposed for a family
placement is to be given similar weight as all other factors in section 37(3)
to be balanced by the court to determine the child’s best interests: see
Childrens’s
Aid Society of Northumberland v. D.P.

[2008] O.J. No. 2047 (Ont. Sup.
Ct.) at para. 126
.

[
197
]

The significance of the child-centered
approach is that good intentions are not enough.  The test is not whether the
parents have seen the light and intend to change, but whether they have in fact
changed and are now able to give the child the care that is in his or her best
interests.  There is not to be experimentation with a child’s life with the result
that in giving the parents another chance, the child would have one less
chance: see
Children’s Aid Society of Winnipeg (City) v. R.

(1980),
1980 CanLII 3654 (MB CA)
, 19 R.F.L. (2d) 232 (Man.C.A.).  There has to be some demonstrated basis
for a determination that the parents are able to parent the child without
endangering his or her safety.  See
Children’s Aid Society of Brockville,
Leeds and Grenville v. C.

[2001] 2001 CarswellOnt 1504
.

[
198
]

Evidence provided about past parenting (not
disputed at this trial) does not mean that it will be admitted.  (Here it was
without objection.)  It must be and I find is relevant.  The probative value
must be tested against the possible prejudice.  The reliability must be clear.
See
Durham CAS v. R.B.

2005 CanLII 32199 (ON SC)
, 2005 O.J. No. 3794 (SCJ).

•

The past parenting evidence must not suffocate
current parental conduct.

•

Factors of reliability are the completeness of
the evidence, has it been tested, the age of the information, the extent to
which it is supported by direct observation of the parent.

•

Are there any guarantees of the reliability?

•

What limits can be put on it, such as limiting
second- or third-hand hearsay?

•

It must be fair and reliable.  See
CAS
Waterloo v. C.R.

1994 CanLII 4520 (ON CTPD)
, 1994 O.J. No. 2955 (OCJ).

[
199
]

Section 7 of the Charter has been applied to
child protection cases.  The use of s. 50 of the
Child and Family Services
Act
must meet the twin tests of necessity and reliability.  In police
reports, direct observations of police officers, but not the statements of
others, may be admitted.  See
CCAS v. L.J.

2003 CanLII 57514 (ON CJ)
, 2003 O.J. No. 1722 (OCJ).

[
200
]

Wider admissibility of evidence was
permitted in
CAS of London and Middlesex v. R.H.

1999 CanLII 14314 (ON SC)
, [1999] O.J. No.
5037 (SCJ).  See also
Catholic Children’s Aid Society of Hamilton v. C.R.
,

2009 CanLII 34047 (ON S.C.D.C.)
, where the court admitted parenting capacity
reports with respect to prior children and stated that: “Neither the fact that
the reports were originally created for use in an earlier court proceeding
concerning the appellants and another child nor the fact that the authors of
the reports have not sworn an affidavit for use on this proceeding is a bar to
admissibility.  The legislature has expressly created a special evidentiary
rule applying to a proceeding under this part of the
Child and Family
Services Act
to permit the admission of such documents.”

[
201
]

It has long been recognized that the
Society, as an agent of the State, is not an ordinary litigant and the
adversarial concept of winning and losing does not apply: see
Re Catholic
Children’s Aid Society of Metropolitan Toronto and P.M.
(1982),
1982 CanLII 1317 (ON PROVCT)
, 36 O.R.
(2d) 451 (Ont. Prov. Ct.).  The Society must act with “fairness and
reasonableness,” exercise good faith, due diligence and reason.  An aggressive
litigation strategy has no part in child protection cases and is contrary to
the Society’s role.  The Society must understand it is the court that
determines the child’s future, relying on the Society to present all relevant
evidence.  The court does not “rubber stamp” decisions previously made by
supervisors or management at the Society.  See
Children’s Aid Society of
Hamilton v. E.O.
,
2009 CanLII 72087 (ON S.C.)
.

[
202
]

Child protection proceedings are unlike
ordinary civil litigation.  The court can choose a flexible approach that would
admit evidence arising at any time up to the date of the court hearing, subject
to adequate disclosure to all parties.  See
CAS Brant v. T (JA.)

2005 ONCJ 302
, and
CAS of Hamilton-Wentworth v. K.R. and C.W.

2001 O.J. No. 5754
.

a)

Only facts related to disposition are
statutorily excluded at the finding phase.

b)

Best interests are paramount.  Child welfare
legislation is different from general legislation and litigation in this
regard.

c)

This approach facilitates an accurate assessment
of present circumstances.

d)

To be overly technical could put the child at
risk.

e)

It prevents multiplicity of proceedings.

f)

Could bring the administration of justice into
disrepute.

g)

Allows parents as well to bring in evidence.

h)

Rigid approach makes it more of a game.  See
further
Brant CAS v. J.A.T.
(2005)
2005 ONCJ 302 (CanLII)
, O.J. No. 5249.

[
203
]

Section 37 of the
Child and Family
Services Act
means a real and not speculative possibility.  Intention is
not necessary.  See
CAS Niagara v. P.T.
(2003),
2003 CanLII 2397 (ON SC)
, 35 RFL 5
th

290.

[
204
]

For example, domestic violence places
children at risk on a number of levels.  Witnessing violence perpetrated
against their mother may have an abusive and detrimental impact on a child’s
development.  Children may feel guilty, blame themselves and feel depressed.

1.

the child’s best interests and include them in the order.  If not, determine

beneficial to the child.  (Section 59(2.1)(a)).  If not both meaningful and

[

In
Children’s Aid Society of Toronto
v. Sheila Ann
, [2005] O.J. No. 2154, 143 A.C.W.S. (3d) 869, [2005]
W.D.F.L. 3688,
2005 ONCJ 274
, 2005 CarswellOnt 2424 (Ont. C.J.), this court
reviewed the insidious impact of domestic violence on women and children.  See
2009
ONCJ 70 (CanLII)
.

[

]

Some excerpts are as follows (my emphasis
added):

[
260
]

[86]

The gravity, indeed, the tragedy of domestic violence can hardly be
overstated.  Expert testimony on the psychological effects of battering
have been admitted in American courts in recent years.  …

[
261
]

[87]

The cycle of violence conforms to the Walker “cycle theory of violence”
named for clinical psychologist Dr. Lenore E. Walker, the pioneer researcher in
the field of the battered wife syndrome.  Dr. Walker first described the
cycle in the book
The Battered Woman
, (New York: Harper Colophon Books,
1979).  In her 1984 book,
The Battered Woman Syndrome
, 2nd ed. (New
York: Springer Publishing Co., 2000), Dr. Walker reported the results of a
study involving 400 battered women.  Her research was designed to test
empirically the theories expounded in her earlier book.

The tension reduction theory states that
there are three distinct phases associated in a recurring battering cycle:
(1) tension building, (2) the acute battering incident, and (3) loving
contrition.  During the first phase, there is a gradual escalation of
tension displayed by discrete acts causing increased friction such as
name-calling, other mean intentional behaviours, and/or physical abuse.
The batterer expresses dissatisfaction and hostility but not in an extreme or
maximally explosive form.  The woman attempts to placate the batterer,
doing what she thinks might please him, calm him down, or at least, what will
not further aggravate him.  She tries not to respond to his hostile
actions and uses general anger reduction techniques.  Often she succeeds
for a little while which reinforces her unrealistic belief that she can
control this man  . . .

[
262
]

[88]

The tension continues to escalate and eventually she is unable to
continue controlling his angry response pattern.  “Exhausted from the
constant stress, she usually withdraws from the batterer, fearing she will
inadvertently set off an explosion.  He begins to move more oppressively
toward her as he observes her withdrawal.  . . .  Tension
between the two becomes unbearable” (Walker, 1979, page 59).  The second
phase, the acute battering incident, becomes inevitable without
intervention.  Sometimes, she precipitates the inevitable explosion so as
to control where and when it occurs, allowing her to take better precautions to
minimize her injuries and pain.

[
263
]

[89]

“Phase two is characterized by the uncontrollable discharge of the
tensions that have built up during phase one” (Walker, 1979, page 59).
The batterer typically unleashes a barrage of verbal and physical aggression
that can leave the woman severely shaken and injured.  In fact, when
injuries do occur, it usually happens during this second phase.  It is
also the time that police become involved, if they are called at all.  The
acute battering phase is concluded when the batterer stops, usually bringing
with its cessation a sharp physiological reduction in tension.  This in
itself is naturally reinforcing.  Violence often succeeds because it does
work.

[
264
]

[90]

In Dr. Walker’s “phase three” which follows, the batterer may apologize
profusely, try to assist his victim, show kindness and remorse and shower her
with gifts and/or promises.  The batterer himself may believe at this
point that he will never allow himself to be violent again.  The woman
wants to believe the batterer and, early in the relationship at least, may
renew her hope in his ability to change.  This third phase provides, for
the woman, the positive reinforcement for remaining in the relationship.
In fact, results showed that phase three could also be characterized by an
absence of tension or violence and no observable loving-contrition behaviour,
and still be reinforcing for the woman.

[
265
]

[91]

Dr. Walker defined a battered woman as a woman who has gone through the
battering cycle at least twice.  As she explained in her introduction to
The
Battered Woman
, at page xv, “Any woman may find herself in an abusive
relationship with a man once.  If it occurs a second time, and she remains
in the situation, she is defined as a battered woman.”

[
266
]

[93]

The partner who becomes battered, if you will, stays in the
relationship probably because of a number of reasons.

[
267
]

[94]

Often in these types of relationships, the person who beats or
assaults, who batters, often tries to make up and begs for forgiveness.
And this individual, who basically has a very disturbed or damaged self-esteem,
all of a sudden feels that he or she — we’ll use women in this case because
it’s so much more common — the spouse feels that she again can do the spouse a
favour and it can make her feel needed and boost her self-esteem for a while
and make her feel worthwhile and the spouse says he’ll forgive her and what
not.

[
268

[95]

to others the fact or extent of the beatings.  I find that as a fact in
the case of Ms. S.A. Co., for example, the lack of hospital records does not
reflect the occasions Ms. S.A. Co. attended at hospitals to be treated for

The mother is internally conflicted as to

typical of victims of domestic violence.  Over time, she has developed some
rational understanding as to the risks that he poses to herself and her

realistic.  I found her evidence fascinating in this regard.  She is in a

cannot reconcile the two.

[
287

and rational further leaves the grandmother with a poor defence mechanism to

[
288

of disengaging from contact or communication with the parents is the
grandmother’s appreciation, or lack thereof, of the assaultive history.  Again,
I see this conflict on two levels.  At times, there is denial and minimization,
then there is rational understanding of the risks that they pose to herself and
the children.  She cannot resolve the two.

[
289

The grandmother has a sense of powerlessness
and is controlled like a remote control car.  Secondly, as a victim she cannot
escape this cycle of violence without significant therapy.  You cannot overcome
this cycle by sheer force of personal will, which is what the grandmother is
primarily relying on to keep her husband and daughter at a distance.

[
290
]

The mother was sexually abused in her
earlier years.  She has not received extensive therapy to deal with those
issues.

[
291
]

The extent and complexity of her trauma is
only now being discovered.  It is arguably evident she requires intensive and
long-term therapy.

[
292
]

The significant delay in obtaining this most
crucial therapy raises the issue of the purpose of society wardship and
supervision orders.

[
293
]

Society wardship is intended to provide
complete protection of children while parents have an opportunity to resolve
their issues.  Society wardship has a time limit implying that parental issues
should be substantially resolved by the outside of the time limit.  Good
progress toward the resolution of the issues during society wardship should
materially reduce the risk factors that brought the children into care in the first
place, thereby making it feasible to manage the lower risk under a supervision
order.

[
294
]

The legislative intent is that we can only
wait so long to rehabilitate parents and risk factors.  Once the time limits
have passed, then the children must be made either crown wards or sent home
under a supervision order.  A custody order is not a realistic option.  I must
dismiss it.

[
295
]

In a high-risk case such as this,
supervision orders are not intended to be the primary vehicle to implement
therapy.  Therapy should commence well before the start of a supervision
order.
It is not the therapy per se that reduces risk to children; it is
the absorption and implementation of the therapy.
Some meaningful
information should be known about implementation, before children become
subject to a supervision order.

[
296
]

Children’s aid societies do not have the
resources to monitor high-risk cases under a supervision order.  They depend
primarily on third-party referrals and plain luck.  The precipitating risk that
led to the children’s being in care should be on a clear, downward trend during
the society wardship phase.  It does not mean that the risk is eliminated,
before the children become subject to a supervision order.  The challenge is at
what point is the risk sufficiently low enough to maintain it under a
supervision order.  If children are sent to their grandmother without reliable
information on risk reduction, then a supervision order becomes an experiment
to determine absorption and implementation of therapy.  This is not the purpose
of a supervision order.

[

assess the absorption and implementation.  We can afford to experiment during
the society wardship phase because the children are well protected in care.

[

Sexual, domestic violence is not simply

circumstances which will protect the child.  When the child cannot be protected
as outlined in the [
Act

strengthening parental rights, but as “fostering the best interests of
children” (p. 191).  L’Heureux-Dubé J. cautioned a p. 191 that “the value of
maintaining a family unit intact [must be] evaluated in contemplation of what

[
320
]

Child protection work is difficult, painful
and complex.  Catering to a child’s best interests in this context means
catering to a vulnerable group at its most vulnerable.  Those who do, do so
knowing that protecting the child’s interests often means doing so at the
expense of the family.  Yet the statutory mandate is to treat the child’s
interests as paramount.  The Society must be free to execute this mandate to
the fullest extent possible.  The result they seek is to restore the child, not
the family.  Where the duties to the child have been performed in accordance
with the statute, there is no ancillary duty to accommodate the family’s wish
for a different result.

[
321
]

The Supreme Court of Canada has held that
“the state’s overriding duty [is] to ensure that children are protected.”
Syl
Apps Secure Treatment Centre v. B.D.
,
2007 SCC 38 (CanLII)
, [2007] 3 S.C.R. 83 (at 87 (QL))
emphasizes the fundamental importance of child development:

A
child’s need for permanency planning without a timeframe sensitive to that
child’s needs demands that the legal process not be used as a strategy to “buy”
a parent time to develop an ability to parent.

…

Child
development does not wait.  Multiple issues of parental dysfunction cannot be
quickly changed.  The child is not to be held in limbo waiting for a change in
a parent that is unlikely to happen.  The parent’s chance to correct parenting
inadequacies must be balanced with a child’s right to appropriate development
within a realistic timeframe if damage to the child is to be minimized.

See
Children’s
Aid Society of Toronto v. R.H.
,
2000 CanLII 3158 (ON CJ)
, [2000] O.J. No. 5853 (QL) (at para.

16

interests of the parent.  See
Nova Scotia (Minister of Community Services)
v. V.T.
,
2008 NSSC 218
, at para.
83
.  It is a child welfare statute (Alberta

T. v. Alberta
(Director of Child Welfare)
,
2000 ABCA 182
, at para.
14
.  Such
legislation may recognize the sanctity of the family and the importance of
keeping the family together, but keeping a family intact is measured in the
context of the best interests of the child, not the parent.  See
G.T.R.
v. D.A.B.

1998 CanLII 29721 (AB PC)

14

CROWN WARDSHIP

[
323
]

Section 57.(1)
Order where child in need
of protection
– Where the court finds that a child is in need of protection
and is satisfied that intervention through a court order is necessary to
protect the child in the future, the court shall make one of the following
orders or an order under section 57.1, in the child’s best interests:

1.

Supervision order
– That the child be placed in the care and custody of a parent or
another person, subject to the supervision of the society, for a specified
period of at least three months and not more than 12 months.

2.

Society wardship
– That the child be made a ward of the society and be placed in its
care and custody for a specified period not exceeding twelve months.

3.

Crown wardship
– That the child be made a ward of the Crown, until the wardship is
terminated under section 65.2 or expires under subsection 71(1), and be placed
in the care of the society.

4.

Consecutive orders of society wardship
and supervision
– That the child be made a ward of
the society under paragraph 2 for a specified period and then be returned to a
parent or another person under paragraph 1, for a period or periods not
exceeding an aggregate of twelve months.

(2)  Court to
inquire –
In determining which order to make under
subsection (1) or section 57.1, the court shall ask the parties what efforts

the society or another agency or person has made to assist the child before
intervention under this Part.

(3)  Less
disruptive alternatives preferred
– The court shall not make an order
removing the child from the care of the person who had charge of him or her
immediately before intervention under this part unless the court is satisfied
that alternatives that are less disruptive to the child, including
non-residential services and the assistance referred to in subsection (2),
would be inadequate to protect the child.

[
324

Crown wardship is a court’s last resort.
The court is required to inquire into the efforts made by the society and other
community services to provide services to the children.  The parent inquiry is
not limited to the timeframe prior to the litigation, but also an inquiry into
the society’s efforts after the removal of the children.  It is a particularly
careful scrutiny when the society ultimately recommends permanent removal.  See

Children and Family Services for York Region v. H.C.
,
2008 CanLII
64678
(SCJ); and
Frontenac CAS v. C.T.

2010 ONSC 3054
.

[
326
]

A Crown Wardship order is the most profound
order that a court can make.  The judge must exercise this only with the
highest degree of caution, and only on the basis of compelling evidence and
after a careful examination of possible alternative remedies.  See
CAS
Hamilton v. M.

2003 O.J. No. 1274
.

[

]

In determining the best interests of the
child, the court must assess the degree to which the risk concerns which
existed when the children came into care, thereafter and now.  See
CAS
Toronto v. C.M.

1994 CanLII 83 (SCC)
, [1994] 2 S.C.R. 165,
supra
.

The significance of the child-centered
approach is that good intentions are not enough.  The test is not whether the
parents have seen the light and intend to change, but whether they have in fact
changed and are now able to give their children the care that is in their best
interests.  Life is not meant to be an experiment with a child’s life with the
result that in giving the parents another chance, the children will have one
less chance.  See
Children’s Aid Society of Winnipeg (City) v. R.

(1980),
1980 CanLII 3654 (MB CA)
, 19 R.F.L. (2d) 232 (Man. C.A.).  There has to be some demonstrated
basis for a determination that the parents are able to parent the child without
endangering his or her safety.  See
Children’s Aid Society of Brockville,
Leeds and Grenville v. C.

[2001] 2001 CarswellOnt 1504
.

“In determining the best interests of the

child’s perspective.
Catholic Children’s Aid Society of Metropolitan
Toronto v. C.M.

1994 CanLII 83 (SCC)
, [1994] 2 S.C.R. 165 (S.C.C.).”  The onus is on the

Ottawa v. C.W. [2008] CanLII 13181 (Sup.Ct.).

The evidentiary onus is on the parents.  A
beneficial relationship is one which is advantageous.  A meaningful
relationship is one which is significant.  It is not enough that there are some
positive aspects to it.  It must be significantly advantageous to the children.
It speaks of an existing relationship, not the possibility of a future
relationship.  Even if the relationship is beneficial and meaningful, there
still must be some qualitative weighing of the benefits of access as opposed to

CAS Niagara v. M.J.

2004 CanLII 2667 (ON SC)
, 2004 O.J. No. 2872.

and S.B.

2002 CanLII 46211 (ON CJ)

The children have had consistent supervised

Because of their young ages and overall
condition, the children are excellent candidates for adoption.  Once a child

Therefore, there will be an order for no

A trial judge is one of the key
decision-makers mandated to promote a child’s best interests.  It has long been
recognized that trial judges are well-positioned to make such key decisions.
See Spence, J. in
Adams v. McLeod
,
1978 CanLII 5 (SCC)
, [1978] 2 S.C.R. 621 at p. 625:

There is
no need to cite any authority to delineate the task of a court upon an infant’s
custody issue.  Time after time, and more particularly through all the latter
part of this century, it has been said and repeated that the one cardinal issue
is the best interest of the infant and that all else is secondary. How then is
that best interest to be determined? Again our courts have been unanimous that
the most authoritative pronouncement thereon is by the trial court judge who
hears the evidence and assesses it.  I commence with the statement by Lord
Simmonds in
McKee v. McKee
,
1951 CanLII 305 (UK JCPC)
, [1951] A.C. 352 (P.C.)], at p. 360:

Further,
it was not, and could not be, disputed that the question of custody of an
infant is a matter which peculiarly lies within the discretion of the judge who
hears the case and has the opportunity generally denied to an appellate
tribunal of seeing the parties and investigating the infant’s circumstances,
and that his decision should not be disturbed unless he has clearly acted on
some wrong principle or disregarded material evidence.
